title: Hydrostatics
summary: Three things carry this subchapter. First, pressure in a static fluid varies only with depth and acts equally in all directions — which makes all of manometry a matter of bookkeeping along a path. Second, the total force on a submerged surface acts at the centre of pressure, which is always BELOW the centroid. Third, a floating body is stable when the metacentre is above the centre of gravity, whereas a fully submerged body needs the centre of buoyancy above the centre of gravity — a distinction examined almost every sitting.

sections.heading: Pressure and its measurement
sections.body:
**Pascal's law:** at a point in a fluid at rest, the **pressure is the same in all directions**. It follows from the fact that a fluid at rest can sustain no shear stress.

**Variation with depth.** In a static fluid,

> **dp/dz = −ρg**,  hence  **p = ρgh = γh**

So pressure depends **only on depth**, not on the shape or volume of the container. Two consequences that questions exploit:

- The pressure at the base of a wide reservoir and of a narrow tube of the same depth is **identical** — the **hydrostatic paradox**.
- All points at the same level in a **connected** body of the same fluid are at the **same pressure**, which is the entire basis of manometry.

**Pressure head** expresses pressure as a height of fluid: **h = p/γ**. The standard equivalences to memorise:

> **Atmospheric pressure = 101.325 kPa = 10.33 m of water = 760 mm of mercury = 1.013 bar**

**Absolute, gauge and vacuum:**

> **p_absolute = p_gauge + p_atmospheric**

| Term | Reference | Sign |
|---|---|---|
| **Absolute** | Perfect vacuum | Always positive |
| **Gauge** | **Local atmospheric** | Positive or negative |
| **Vacuum** | Atmospheric, measured downward | = negative gauge pressure |

Unless a question says otherwise, **pressures are gauge** — the convention throughout engineering practice.

**Instruments, and which reads what:**

| Instrument | Reads |
|---|---|
| **Barometer** | **Absolute (atmospheric)** pressure |
| **Piezometer** | Moderate positive gauge pressure of a liquid |
| **Simple manometer** | Gauge pressure at a point |
| **Differential manometer** | **Difference** of pressure between two points |
| **Inverted / inclined manometer** | Small differences, magnified |
| Bourdon gauge | Gauge pressure, mechanically |

The **barometer** is the one to notice: it is the only instrument in the list reading **absolute** pressure, and "which instrument measures atmospheric pressure" is a standard question.

**Manometry method.** Work along a path from the known pressure to the unknown, **adding γh going down and subtracting γh going up**, and remembering that pressure is unchanged when moving **horizontally within one continuous fluid**. That single procedure solves every manometer problem without a separate formula.

An **inclined** manometer magnifies a small reading: a vertical rise h appears as a length **L = h/sin θ** along the tube, so a shallow inclination gives high resolution — the standard device for measuring small air-pressure differences.

sections.heading: Total pressure and centre of pressure
sections.body:
For a **plane surface** immersed in a liquid:

> **Total pressure F = γ A h̄**

where **h̄** is the depth of the **centroid** of the area. So the total force is simply the pressure at the centroid multiplied by the area.

But the force does **not act at the centroid**. It acts at the **centre of pressure**:

> **h_cp = h̄ + I_G /(A h̄)**   (vertical surface)
> **h_cp = h̄ + I_G sin²θ /(A h̄)**   (surface inclined at θ to the horizontal)

**The centre of pressure is ALWAYS below the centroid**, because the added term I_G/(Ah̄) is always positive. The physical reason: pressure **increases with depth**, so the lower part of the surface carries more than its share of the force, pulling the resultant downward.

Two useful special cases:

| Surface | h̄ | h_cp |
|---|---|---|
| **Vertical rectangle**, top edge at the free surface, depth d | d/2 | **2d/3** |
| Vertical rectangle, fully submerged | Depends | Approaches h̄ as depth increases |
| **Horizontal** surface | Uniform pressure | **Coincides with the centroid** |

The first is worth memorising outright: for a vertical gate or wall retaining water to its top, the resultant acts at **two thirds of the depth from the surface**, that is **d/3 from the base**. It is the same result as the triangular earth pressure distribution, for the same reason — a triangular loading has its centroid at one third of the height.

Note also that **as the surface is submerged deeper, the centre of pressure approaches the centroid**, because I_G/(Ah̄) shrinks as h̄ grows. A deeply submerged gate is loaded almost uniformly.

**Curved surfaces** are handled by resolving into components rather than by a single formula:

| Component | Equals |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal force F_H** | The force on the **vertical projection** of the surface |
| **Vertical force F_V** | The **weight of the liquid** contained above the surface (real or imaginary) |

The resultant is **√(F_H² + F_V²)** at **tan⁻¹(F_V/F_H)** to the horizontal. The vertical component being a *weight* is the elegant part: for a surface with liquid above it the weight is real, and for one with liquid below it the weight is that of the imaginary volume that would sit above.

**Where this is applied:** dam and retaining-wall design, **sluice gates**, **lock gates**, tank walls, and the **pressure on an immersed body**. For a **dam**, the horizontal water thrust ½γH² acting at H/3 is the primary overturning force, resisted by the dam's own weight — and the **no-tension (middle third) rule** e ≤ B/6 then governs the base width.

sections.heading: Buoyancy and flotation
sections.body:
**Archimedes' principle:** a body wholly or partly immersed experiences an **upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced**, acting through the **centre of buoyancy** — which is the **centroid of the displaced volume**, not of the body.

Two distinct cases, and mixing them is a standard error:

| Body | Displaces |
|---|---|
| **Floating** | Its **own WEIGHT** of fluid |
| **Fully submerged** | Its **own VOLUME** of fluid |

That single distinction settles most flotation problems immediately. A floating body sinks until the displaced weight equals its own; a submerged body's buoyancy is fixed by its volume and cannot adjust.

**Conditions of equilibrium:**

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Weight > buoyancy | **Sinks** |
| Weight = buoyancy | **Neutral** — floats submerged at any depth |
| Weight < buoyancy | **Rises** until partly emerged, then floats |

**Stability — and here the two cases differ fundamentally.**

For a **fully submerged** body (a submarine, a balloon), the centre of buoyancy **B is fixed relative to the body**, because the displaced volume is the whole body and cannot change shape. So:

> **Submerged body: stable when B is ABOVE G.**

For a **floating** body, tilting changes the **shape of the displaced volume**, so **B moves sideways**. The vertical through the new B intersects the original axis at the **metacentre M**, and:

> **Floating body: stable when M is ABOVE G**, that is when **GM is positive**.

This is the distinction examined almost every sitting: **B above G for a submerged body, M above G for a floating one.** A floating body can be perfectly stable with **G above B** — a ship normally is — because the shift of buoyancy on tilting generates a **righting couple**.

**Metacentric height:**

> **GM = I/V − BG**

where **I** is the second moment of area of the **water-line plane** about the axis of tilt and **V** the displaced volume. The term **I/V = BM** is the metacentric radius.

Note what I/V means physically: a **wide** vessel has a large water-line I, hence a large BM and good stability. That is why barges and catamarans are stable and why a narrow deep hull is not.

**Determining GM experimentally** by moving a known weight w through a distance x across the deck and measuring the resulting tilt θ:

> **GM = w x / (W tan θ)**

**Large or small GM?** A larger GM gives a **stiffer, more stable** vessel — but also a **shorter, jerkier rolling period**, since

> **T = 2π √(k²/(g · GM))**

so T falls as GM rises. Passenger comfort and cargo safety therefore call for a **moderate** GM, not the largest possible: an over-stiff ship rolls violently and can shift or damage its cargo. This trade-off is a favourite conceptual question.

**Three states**, for completeness: **stable** (M above G, GM positive), **unstable** (M below G, GM negative — the body capsizes), and **neutral** (M coincides with G).

A practical civil-engineering application is the **buoyancy raft** and the check on **uplift of empty tanks and basements**: a below-ground structure lighter than the water it displaces will **float**, which has happened to more than one empty swimming pool and sewage tank.

formulas.label: Hydrostatic pressure
formulas.expression: p = ρgh = γh ;   p_absolute = p_gauge + p_atmospheric
formulas.note: Depends only on depth. Atmospheric = 101.325 kPa = 10.33 m water = 760 mm Hg.

formulas.label: Total pressure on a plane surface
formulas.expression: F = γ A h̄     (h̄ = depth of the CENTROID)
formulas.note: The pressure at the centroid times the area — but the force does not act there.

formulas.label: Centre of pressure
formulas.expression: h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄) ;   inclined: h_cp = h̄ + I_G sin²θ/(A h̄)
formulas.note: ALWAYS below the centroid, because pressure increases with depth. For a vertical rectangle to the surface: 2d/3.

formulas.label: Force on a curved surface
formulas.expression: F_H = force on the vertical projection ;   F_V = weight of liquid above (real or imaginary)

formulas.label: Archimedes' principle
formulas.expression: Buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced, acting through the centre of buoyancy
formulas.note: A FLOATING body displaces its own weight; a SUBMERGED body its own volume.

formulas.label: Metacentric height
formulas.expression: GM = I/V − BG ;   experimentally GM = w x /(W tan θ)
formulas.note: I is of the water-line plane. Floating body stable when M is above G; submerged body when B is above G.

formulas.label: Rolling period
formulas.note: A larger GM means more stability but a shorter, jerkier roll — so a moderate GM is preferred.
